title: Breakfast by the Sea and Peter Restored
summary: Back in Galilee, seven disciples fish all night and catch nothing until the risen Jesus, unrecognized on the shore, tells them where to cast the net. He feeds them breakfast by a charcoal fire, then asks Peter three times whether he loves him and three times commissions him to feed his sheep, foretelling the death by which Peter will glorify God. The Gospel ends by identifying the beloved disciple as its witness and author.
story: John 20 closed with what reads like the end of the book (20:30-31). Chapter 21 is an epilogue that ties up two threads left hanging. The first is Peter: he denied Jesus three times beside a charcoal fire (18:18, 25-27), and though he has seen the risen Lord, nothing has yet been said about his failure. The second is the future: what will become of the disciples, and in particular of Peter and the beloved disciple, now that Jesus is going to the Father. The chapter returns to Galilee, where it all began, to ordinary work and an ordinary meal, and there Jesus restores a failed disciple and sends him out as a shepherd.
historical:
The Sea of Tiberias is the Sea of Galilee, a freshwater lake about thirteen miles long in northern Israel. It took this name from the city of Tiberias, which Herod Antipas founded on its western shore around AD 20 in honor of the emperor Tiberius; John uses it as the name his readers would know. Fishing was a major industry around the lake, and several of Jesus' disciples had worked in it.

Scholars debate how chapter 21 came to be part of the Gospel. Many think it was added after the main work was finished, perhaps by the author himself or by those who knew him, since 21:24 speaks of the disciple in the third person and adds “we know that his testimony is true.” Others see it as a planned epilogue balancing the prologue of chapter 1. What is certain is that no surviving manuscript of John lacks it. Verses 18 and 19 point to Peter's martyrdom; early Christian writers report that he died in Rome under the emperor Nero in the mid-60s AD, and later tradition says by crucifixion. The rumor that the beloved disciple would not die (21:23) suggests he lived to an old age and that his death, or approaching death, needed explaining.
cultural:
Night was the best time for net fishing on the lake. Fishermen worked in light clothing or stripped for the work, which is why Peter wraps his outer garment around himself before leaping into the water, an odd but natural detail. A hundred yards is literally two hundred cubits, a cubit being the length of a forearm. Sharing a meal was an act of fellowship and acceptance in the ancient world, and a host who served his guests with his own hands honored them.

The charcoal fire deliberately recalls the fire in the high priest's courtyard; the Greek word occurs only in these two places in the New Testament. Shepherding was the Old Testament's great image for leadership: kings and priests were meant to be shepherds of Israel, and Ezekiel 34 condemns the shepherds who fed themselves instead of the flock. When Jesus tells Peter to feed and shepherd his sheep, he entrusts him with the care that Jesus himself, the good shepherd of chapter 10, has shown.
literary: The chapter has two halves: a miracle scene (1-14) and a dialogue scene (15-23), followed by a closing testimony (24-25). The catch of fish echoes the call of the first disciples in Luke 5:1-11, and the meal of bread and fish echoes the feeding of the five thousand (John 6). The dialogue is built on threes: three questions, three answers, three commissions, answering Peter's three denials. The number 153 has attracted many symbolic readings, from the ancient observation (made by Augustine) that it is the sum of the numbers 1 through 17 to the idea that it stands for all the nations; John gives no hint of symbolism, and it may simply be the remembered count of an astonished eyewitness. The book's last verse, with its world too small for the books, is a deliberate overstatement of wonder, the author's closing bow.

outline.t: Seven disciples go fishing and catch nothing
Jesus on the shore and the great catch
Do you love Me? Peter restored and commissioned
The witness and the many untold things

doctrines.note: Jesus does not ignore Peter's denial or shame him for it. He reopens the wound gently, with three questions matching three failures, and brings Peter to confess his love again. Restoration in this chapter comes through honest facing of failure in the presence of mercy.

The risen Jesus entrusts his flock to human shepherds. Peter's commission to feed and shepherd the sheep shows that the church's leaders serve people who belong to Christ (My lambs, My sheep), not to themselves.

Jesus tells Peter how he will die and refuses to satisfy his curiosity about the beloved disciple. Each disciple has his own calling and end under the Lord's hand. The command is the same for both: Follow Me.

words.note: Agapao, to love. In the first two questions Jesus uses agapao, and Peter answers with phileo; in the third Jesus uses phileo. Some interpreters see a deliberate contrast between a higher, self-giving love and a lesser affection. Many others note that John uses the two verbs interchangeably elsewhere (the Father loves the Son with both, 3:35 and 5:20) and read the change as stylistic variation. On either reading, the point of the scene is the threefold question matching the threefold denial.

Phileo, to love, often with the sense of friendship or affection. Peter uses it in all three answers, and Peter's grief in verse 17 comes because Jesus asked a third time, not because of a change in verb. The word is related to philos, friend, the word Jesus used when he told his disciples he no longer called them servants but friends (15:15).

Poimaino, to shepherd, which includes feeding but also guiding, protecting, and ruling. Jesus' three commands alternate between feeding and shepherding, lambs and sheep. The same verb is used in 1 Peter 5:2, where Peter urges elders to shepherd God's flock willingly, perhaps remembering this morning.

christ: The risen Christ in this chapter is the same Lord who called fishermen, fed the hungry, and washed feet. He comes to his disciples in the middle of their failure (a fruitless night), provides abundantly, and serves them breakfast. He knows all things, as Peter says, including the depths of Peter's love and weakness, and still entrusts him with his flock. He is Lord of the future as well, able to say how Peter will glorify God in death and whether the beloved disciple will remain until he returns. The phrase until I return is a clear statement of the hope of Christ's coming again. And the final call, Follow Me, is the same word with which the Gospels begin the life of discipleship.

hard.q: Who is the beloved disciple who wrote this Gospel, and can his testimony be trusted?
hard.a:
The Gospel never names him. Church tradition from the late second century identifies him with John the son of Zebedee, one of the Twelve, and this remains a widely held view; the sons of Zebedee are present in 21:2, and John is otherwise surprisingly absent by name from this Gospel. Other scholars propose a disciple from Jerusalem who was not one of the Twelve (sometimes linked with an early figure called John the Elder), or Lazarus, whom Jesus is said to love (11:3, 5). Some think a circle of the disciple's followers shaped the final text, as the we of 21:24 may suggest.

On any of these views the Gospel claims to rest on eyewitness testimony, and it is candid about the failures of its witnesses, including Peter's denial and Thomas's doubt. Scholars such as Richard Bauckham (Jesus and the Eyewitnesses, 2006) have argued that the Gospel's claim to eyewitness authority should be taken seriously as a historical claim. Readers will weigh that claim differently, but the Gospel asks to be read as testimony, not as legend.

questions: Jesus meets Peter by a charcoal fire, the same kind of fire where Peter denied him. Why might Jesus bring him back to that memory rather than avoid it?
Peter's restoration comes with a task: feed My sheep. How does being forgiven relate to being given responsibility for others?
Peter asks, What about him? and Jesus answers, what is that to you? Where does comparison with others distract you from following Jesus yourself?
